items.title: OpenAI partners with Google Cloud to offer frontier models and Codex workflows through Google Cloud's Model Garden and Marketplace [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenAI models are coming to Google Cloud
items.summary:
OpenAI and Google Cloud have partnered to integrate OpenAI's frontier models and Codex agentic workflows into Google Cloud's Model Garden, enabling customers to access these models natively within Google Cloud's infrastructure. This integration supports complex AI workflows at scale while providing enterprises with data governance and access controls suited for regulated industries.

The models will be available for purchase through the Google Cloud Marketplace, allowing enterprises with Google Cloud spend commitments to apply those credits. OpenAI models will also be accessible via Google Antigravity and the Gemini Agent, offering customers flexibility in model selection. General availability is planned in the coming weeks, expanding enterprise options for deploying frontier AI models within Google Cloud environments.

items.title: OpenAI leads global coalition to coordinate response and patch critical PHP vulnerabilities discovered by AI agents [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Patch the Planet: global response coordination as agents uncover vulnerabilities
items.summary:
OpenAI coordinated with PHP maintainers, security researchers, and providers to address critical vulnerabilities found in the PHP programming language using AI models like GPT-5.6 Sol. The coalition included partners such as Wiz and Cloudflare, focusing on preparing fixes, testing, and deploying protections ahead of public disclosure to mitigate widespread risk.

The initiative, called Patch the Planet, involved validating vulnerabilities, developing patches, and coordinating with infrastructure providers and government agencies to protect critical systems. OpenAI also committed $1 billion in subsidized AI model access to support frontline defenders with limited security resources. This effort highlights both the potential and risks of AI in cybersecurity, as AI can uncover flaws faster than attackers but also accelerate exploit development.

OpenAI proposes a scalable framework for coordinated vulnerability response in the AI era, emphasizing collaboration among maintainers, researchers, providers, and governments to manage the increasing pace of AI-discovered security issues in widely used software.

items.title: Report: Texas data center expansion could triple soot and double smog pollution by 2031, reversing decades of air quality improvements [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Data centers could erase decades of air quality gains
items.summary:
A surge in new data centers in Texas, driven by demand for generative AI infrastructure, could significantly increase air pollution to levels not seen since the early 2000s. The Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC) warns that if these data centers rely on the current electricity grid mix, emissions of fine particle pollution and smog-forming nitrogen oxides could more than double within five years, erasing years of air quality progress.

Texas leads the US in data center capacity with 26 gigawatts existing or under construction and is expected to add more onsite power generation, often using gas turbines that are less efficient and more polluting. HARC's modeling shows that pairing grid power with onsite renewable energy could reduce emissions substantially, but reliance on gas engines could result in the highest pollution scenarios. The report highlights the risk that air quality gains achieved over decades could be undone if cleaner energy solutions are not prioritized in data center development.

items.title: Alter launches privileged access management platform for AI agents with per-agent keys, policy enforcement, and audit trails [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Launch HN: Alter (YC S25) – Access control for multi-user agents
items.summary:
Alter has introduced a privileged access management platform designed for AI agents that enables control over agent actions on behalf of users. The platform provides per-agent identities and scoped credentials, enforces policies including human approvals, and maintains tamper-evident audit logs for every action.

The system stores credentials securely in a vault and injects them per request, preventing exposure in code or environment files. It supports integrations with LangChain, MCP, and AWS, and offers features such as default-deny policies, instant revocation, and compliance-ready audit trails. Alter aims to help teams pass security reviews and maintain strict access controls for multi-user AI agents.

items.title: LiteLLM patches security breach after attacker pushed malware in v1.107.0 Docker and PyPI releases on October 21, 2026 [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LiteLLM Security Update
items.summary:
LiteLLM confirmed a security incident on October 21, 2026, when its release pipeline was compromised, resulting in a malicious v1.107.0 version being published to Docker Hub and PyPI. This version contained malware designed to steal credentials and enable remote code execution. The affected releases were live for a limited time before being pulled, and all previous versions remain safe. Enterprise customers using the private LiteLLM registry were not impacted.

The compromised artifacts included multiple Docker images and PyPI packages available between approximately 11:39 and 14:20 UTC. LiteLLM identified the attack chain involved multiple security control breaches. Users who installed or ran the affected versions are advised to assume compromise, remove malicious files, and downgrade to version 1.106.2 or earlier. The company continues investigating the incident and has provided detailed guidance for detection and remediation.

items.title: Meta, Sierra, and partners launch Personal Agent Protocol to standardize secure interactions between personal AI agents and businesses [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Personal Agent Protocol
items.summary:
Meta, Sierra, and industry partners including Genesys, Instinct, Rocket, Shopify, Stripe, and Walmart have introduced the Personal Agent Protocol, an open standard designed to enable personal AI agents to interact securely and efficiently with businesses. The protocol aims to improve interoperability by allowing consumers to control agent access while giving companies visibility and control over agent actions through websites, APIs, or company agents.

The protocol uses OAuth for authorization and supports multiple connection methods, including websites, APIs built on standards like MCP and OpenAPI, and conversational agents for complex tasks. It is designed to enhance user experience by speeding up tasks such as scheduling, shopping, and customer support, while maintaining privacy and security. The developers plan to publish the initial specification and reference implementation soon and invite further collaboration to expand features like detailed permissions, push notifications, and payment extensions.

items.title: Blackstone’s Jas Khaira says concerns over AI infrastructure debt are exaggerated amid rising interest rates and market jitters [ * ] [ ◼ ]

items.summary:
Blackstone is heavily investing in AI infrastructure through its Blackstone N1 group, led by Jas Khaira, who emphasizes the firm's unique approach to financing AI compute with flexible capital structures. Despite recent market concerns about the large debt burdens of AI-focused neocloud providers like CoreWeave and Firmus, Khaira argues that fears are overblown, citing strong customer contracts and the ongoing high demand for compute resources.

Khaira explained that rising interest rates and credit spreads have increased borrowing costs even for major tech companies, contributing to market volatility and the cancellation of Firmus' IPO. However, Blackstone continues to support AI infrastructure buildout, viewing its $1.3 trillion in assets as critical to meeting the capital-intensive needs of the AI transition.

items.title: Report: AI agent deletes entire edit of Swedish TV show The Challenge weeks before release due to failed backup system [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Unsupervised AI agent reportedly deletes TV show's edit before release
items.summary:
The Swedish edition of the athletic competition show The Challenge lost months of editing work when an AI agent deleted the finished season from the production server just weeks before its release. The program director attributed the incident to a failed backup system, which prevented recovery of the deleted files and forced the production team to re-edit the entire season from raw footage.

According to sources cited by Aftonbladet, the AI agent had file-handling permissions on the production server and deleted the completed edit, though the exact role of the AI agent remains unclear. TV4, the show's commissioner, conducted an investigation and stated the mishap was due to human error rather than autonomous AI action. The incident highlights risks associated with AI file management and backup failures in media production environments.

items.title: Recursive launches Flint, a free laptop-sized coding model largely developed by its AI research system, as an early test of AI self-improvement [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Recursive launches Flint, a laptop coding model it says was largely built by AI
items.summary:
Recursive, an AI startup founded last year, has released Flint, a free coding model designed to run on laptops that was largely built using its own AI research system called the Eureka Machine. This model represents an early public test of recursive self-improvement, where AI assists in building better AI under human supervision.

Flint uses a mixture-of-experts architecture with 40 billion parameters but activates only 2.5 billion at a time, making it lightweight enough for ordinary laptops. It outperforms similar-sized models on coding benchmarks and runs faster on devices like the MacBook Pro with Apple’s M4 Pro chip. Recursive aims for the Eureka Machine to progressively improve its research capabilities, potentially enabling more autonomous AI development in the future while maintaining human oversight.

items.title: Databricks launches AI Runtime with managed GPU infrastructure for scalable, secure enterprise AI model training [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Databricks launches AI Runtime for managed GPU training on enterprise data
items.summary:
Databricks has launched AI Runtime (AIR), a managed service that integrates high-performance GPU infrastructure directly into its platform to enable scalable and secure training of AI models on enterprise data. AIR aims to reduce operational overhead by providing serverless, on-demand GPU access with built-in governance through Unity Catalog, allowing teams to focus on model development without managing GPU infrastructure separately.

The service offers features such as near-instant launch latency, environment caching, and debugging tools compatible with major AI frameworks including Ray. Hundreds of companies across industries like healthcare and manufacturing are already using AIR to accelerate deep learning model training and deployment. AIR also integrates with Databricks' Lakeflow for pipeline orchestration and supports multi-node training with optimized performance and workload isolation to protect sensitive data.

items.title: Walmart launches Agent Gateway to enable AI agents to shop with user controls, contrasting Amazon's ban on AI agent purchases [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: While Amazon blocks AI agents, Walmart rolls out the welcome mat
items.summary:
Walmart has introduced its Agent Gateway, a new platform allowing AI agents to make purchases on behalf of customers with spending controls and transaction approvals. This move follows Amazon's decision to block AI agents from shopping on its site, positioning Walmart as a leader in agentic commerce.

The Agent Gateway uses the model context protocol to connect approved AI agents to Walmart's inventory, enabling shopping without sharing personal data directly with the agents. Walmart also plans to roll out Agent Profiles that let customers authorize agents, monitor purchases separately, and set spending limits or approval requirements.

Walmart's approach includes specific terms for AI agents to ensure they act within customer intentions, restrict access to payment information, and comply with return policies. Agents violating these terms will be blocked, aiming to provide a secure and user-friendly experience as AI-driven shopping becomes more mainstream.

items.title: Anthropic launches Claude Duet AI agent for professionals and small businesses as a research preview on iOS, Android, and web [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Anthropic takes on Muse with Claude Duet, its new AI agent
items.summary:
Anthropic has introduced Claude Duet, a new AI agent designed for professionals and small business owners, available as a research preview. The agent operates on Claude Opus 5.5 and can manage tasks ranging from scheduling meetings to building dashboards and financial forecasts, sending users daily briefs and alerts only when necessary.

Claude Duet integrates memory, skills, and connected apps from Claude and includes a virtual machine with browsing capabilities. It requires user approval before performing sensitive actions and employs a safety system to protect sensitive information like credit card numbers. Currently, it is an early version with some limitations, such as occasional misreading of priorities and weaker performance on personal errands. Access is limited to Pro or Max subscribers in the US via a waitlist.

items.title: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg agrees to remain in California for eight years under new stock agreement amid potential billionaire tax ballot measure [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Mark Zuckerberg Agrees to Stay in California Despite Billionaires’ Tax Ballot Measure
items.summary:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has agreed to stay in California for eight years despite considering a move due to a proposed ballot measure that would impose a one-time 5 percent tax on billionaires' stock and assets. The agreement, reached with Meta's board, links his ability to sell special nonvoting shares to his continued residence in the state, aiming to keep him close to the company's AI development efforts in Silicon Valley.

The decision follows concerns from a special committee of Meta's board about the challenges faced when Zuckerberg was not physically present during the COVID-19 pandemic. The new class of shares created under the agreement could help fund Meta's AI investments without diluting Zuckerberg's voting control. While the agreement allows for relocation if Meta moves its headquarters, recent polling suggests the tax measure may not pass, potentially reducing the immediate tax impact on Zuckerberg.

items.title: Researchers develop multi-agent large language model system to coordinate and play Pokémon Showdown 2v2 battles, demonstrating improved performance with agent communication [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LLM Agents Play Pokemon Showdown
items.summary:
Researchers have created a multi-agent environment using large language models (LLMs) to play Pokémon Showdown's 2v2 format, focusing on how agents coordinate, communicate, and strategize together. The system allows agents to exchange messages and choose moves based on a plain-English summary of the battle, aiming to evaluate collaborative behaviors in a game-theory setting with hidden information and randomness.

Experiments showed that agents who communicated freely won 64% of battles against a scripted max-damage bot, outperforming agents with limited or no communication. The environment uses the official Pokémon Showdown simulator and supports different communication modes, serving as a benchmark for comparing model capabilities and potentially training agents with reinforcement learning to enhance collaboration. The project highlights the importance of agent interaction in multi-agent AI systems and plans to develop a leaderboard and further research on communication effects.

items.title: Thoma Bravo-backed Proofpoint to acquire Varonis Systems for $6.3 billion at a discount amid rising cybersecurity M&A activity [ * ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Thoma Bravo Found a Discount in a Hot Cybersecurity Market
items.summary: Thoma Bravo's cybersecurity firm Proofpoint agreed to acquire data security company Varonis Systems for $6.3 billion, valuing Varonis at about six times forward annual recurring revenue, below comparable public peers. This deal highlights how private equity can still find opportunities in the competitive cybersecurity market despite rising interest rates and high corporate acquisition activity. The acquisition expands Proofpoint's offerings beyond email threat protection to include data security and access control, positioning it for potential future growth and an IPO. The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027, with Thoma Bravo planning additional large cybersecurity acquisitions focused on AI-driven revenue models.

items.originalSummary:
Cybersecurity has been a dealmaking bright spot amid the broader software gloom, fueled by bets that AI adoption will boost demand for security products. But it’s been hard for private equity firms to get in on the sizzling sector. 

Corporate buyers have been snapping up cybersecurity companies, competition that makes it harder for private equity firms to buy at prices that leave room for attractive returns when they eventually sell. Rising interest rates further limit what the firms can pay in debt-heavy buyouts. 

That makes Thoma Bravo–backed cybersecurity company Proofpoint’s agreement last week to acquire data security company Varonis Systems in a $6.3 billion deal a notable example of how private equity can still find an opening in a hot market. And the tech-focused private equity giant is likely to do at least one more deal around this size in the coming year. 

The proposed acquisition values Varonis at around six times forward annual recurring revenue, according to a person close to the deal. That’s a discount compared to similar public companies like cloud security and compliance company Qualys, which is trading at around 8 times forward annual recurring revenue. 

Cybersecurity acquisitions were already booming heading into this year, including Alphabet’s $32 billion agreement to buy Wiz and Palo Alto Networks’ roughly $25 billion deal for CyberArk, both announced in 2025. But interest in the sector has intensified amid much-hyped releases of powerful models like Anthropic’s Mythos and a series of hacking incidents and agents gone rogue. It could further increase after Wednesday’s disclosure of AI finding a security flaw in open-source programming language PHP, which most websites use.

“People ended up realizing that the...threat vector effectively multiplied to infinity,” said Brian Thom, a managing director at middle market investment bank Brown Gibbons Lang & Co. with a focus on infrastructure software and cybersecurity.

Cybersecurity mergers and acquisitions hit a record 170 transactions in Europe and North America during the third quarter, according to an Arrowpoint Advisory report from earlier this month. Corporate buyers have been particularly active, including Accenture, which this summer acquired a majority stake in industrial cybersecurity company Dragos, plus two smaller companies in deals with a combined enterprise value of more than $4 billion. 

Thoma Bravo, for its part, saw an opportunity as Varonis’ stock price came under pressure. Varonis has spent recent years moving customers from licenses to cloud-based subscriptions, temporarily depressing revenue growth, and announced late last year it would phase out older software by the end of 2026. Its shares had tumbled nearly 50% from last October to around $33 this June, right before reports of a potential takeover surfaced. 

More broadly, some software-focused private equity firms are hunting for companies with depressed share prices but still-credible growth prospects that can hold up even under threat of AI disruption. And many are still nursing the hangover from a software binge during the low-interest-rate years of 2020 and 2021. 

The Varonis acquisition comes at a critical time for Thoma Bravo, which has owned Proofpoint since taking it over for $12.3 billion in 2021. Proofpoint is generating more than $1 billion in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, excluding the proposed Varonis acquisition, the person said, while five years under Thoma Bravo ownership puts it at the point when private equity firms typically face growing pressure to cash out. 

Adding Varonis expands Proofpoint’s capabilities beyond its traditional focus of protecting employees from cyberattacks, including phishing and other email threats, to securing sensitive corporate data and controlling who can access it, including employees and AI agents. Though Proofpoint has made previous acquisitions under Thoma Bravo, the Varonis deal is by far its largest and gives it a bigger foothold in AI-related defenses that could arguably help it become a more compelling candidate for an initial public offering. 

Thoma Bravo could be on the hunt for more multibillion-dollar cybersecurity acquisitions following the Varonis deal, which is set to close in the first half of 2027. 

“There’s a finite number of very large cybercompanies that we can invest in,” said Andrew Almeida, a Thoma Bravo partner who oversees cybersecurity and infrastructure software investments. 

The firm is particularly interested in companies that generate revenue from the growing use of AI agents rather than relying solely on traditional pricing models that charge based on the number of human users, he said, and it plans to have another deal similar to the size of Varonis within the next 12 months. 

“Having agentic revenue, not just an agentic vision, but agentic revenue, is a must. And then having a pricing model that can capture this upcoming and ongoing explosion of agents is also a must,” Almeida added. 

Wobbly IPO Window

All eyes are on when Anthropic will finally make its IPO paperwork public, marking one of the final steps toward its hotly anticipated debut. Anthropic announced it had confidentially filed in June, and by late summer was preparing for an IPO as soon as late September.  Now the latest chatter is that the filing could appear by the end of this week. 

Other AI-related IPOs that initially looked poised to go ahead of Anthropic’s have been pulled or delayed amid mounting concerns about the costs of financing data centers and chips, while the broader IPO market has lost momentum in the midst of Treasury volatility. That’s raised questions about who will test the market next—and whether Anthropic’s offering could revive IPOs in general. Some IPO advisers, however, say other companies may need to go public first, paving the way for the AI giant. 

“I don’t think Anthropic going public is going to open the floodgates,” said Edward Best, co-chair of Willkie Farr & Gallagher’s capital markets practice. “I think that Anthropic is going to wait until the water starts moving, and then if Anthropic comes through, it’s just going to widen the river.

“They can’t take the risk that they don’t do well. They’re going to wait until they see a better path, and then other people are going to join right afterwards,” he added.

items.title: Walmart to allow AI agents to shop on its website with user approval and spending limits starting next month [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Walmart is inviting AI agents to shop for you
items.summary:
Walmart will enable customers to use AI agents to shop on its website beginning next month, implementing controls that require user approval for purchases and allow setting spending limits. The company has established rules to ensure AI agents act only within the shopper's intent and restrict access to necessary information, blocking agents that violate these terms. This move contrasts with Amazon's approach, which has blocked similar AI shopping assistants.

Walmart's system includes an "Agent Gateway" that connects AI agents through an open standard called the Model Context Protocol, facilitating smoother shopping experiences without exposing customers' full shopping histories. Users can manage AI agent activity through "Agent Profiles," reviewing purchases separately and disabling agents at any time. The feature will also be available on Sam's Club, reflecting Walmart's broader embrace of AI shopping assistants while maintaining user control and privacy.

items.title: NSA warns of critical PHP vulnerabilities found by OpenAI and Google’s Wiz, urging immediate patching of millions of websites [ ! ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: PHP Armageddon: OpenAI, Google’s Wiz find ancient holes, panicking the internet
items.summary:
The U.S. National Security Agency issued a warning about two severe security flaws in PHP, a server-side language powering about 70% of websites, including WordPress sites. These vulnerabilities, present since PHP version 5 released in 2004, allow attackers to access server file systems or databases, prompting the NSA to recommend taking unpatched sites offline until fixed.

OpenAI and Google’s Wiz discovered the flaws using AI tools as part of responsible security research, collaborating with the PHP Foundation and major tech companies to develop and test patches. While no exploits have been reported yet, AI now lowers the barrier for attackers to adapt exploits across PHP versions, making rapid patching critical to protect millions of websites from potential attacks.

items.title: SZED submits multi-task label-attention and cross-modal fusion model for Arabic hateful meme detection in ArGuard 2026 Track A [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SZED at ArGuard Shared Tasks: Multi-Task Label-Attention and Cross-Modal Fusion for Arabic Hateful Meme Detection
items.summary:
SZED presented their model for the ArGuard 2026 Track A challenge on Arabic hateful meme detection, which involves binary classification and fine-grained multi-label tagging. Their approach combines MARBERTv2 and CLIP ViT-L/14 embeddings for classification and uses a multi-task label-attention architecture with per-class query vectors and cascade calibration for tagging, achieving macro-F1 scores of 0.7597 and 0.3142 respectively.

The team compared different fusion methods including concatenation, self-attention, and ensemble heads for the classification task and analyzed reproducibility, per-class error patterns, and the impact of cascade calibration on the long-tailed label distribution in the tagging task.

The task has two parts: binary classification (A1) and fine-grained multi-label tagging (A2). For A1, we fuse MARBERTv2 and CLIP ViT-L/14 embeddings, comparing concatenation, self-attention, and ensemble heads. items.title: Researchers introduce MEDIATOR, an ontology-agnostic tokenizer for EHR modeling that improves clinical prediction and zero-shot transfer across health systems [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Discrete Neural Interlingua for Ontology-Agnostic EHR Modeling
items.summary: Researchers present MEDIATOR, a discrete tokenizer that maps clinical concepts from text into a shared vector-quantized codebook, enabling open-vocabulary tokenization without manual mappings or fixed vocabularies. MEDIATOR addresses the tokenization bottleneck in electronic health record (EHR) foundation models by collapsing equivalent expressions and organizing distinct concepts in a medically meaningful discrete space. When used with an EHR Transformer, MEDIATOR improves prediction accuracy on 20 MIMIC-III tasks and shows significant gains in zero-shot transfer to 14 eICU tasks, utilizing all events where previous models could only use a fraction. The model's design enhances transfer robustness, entity-linking quality, and enables transferable attribution across hospitals, supporting scalable clinical prediction across diverse health systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.27047v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: EHR foundation models promise scalable clinical prediction across health systems, yet their deployment is constrained by a tokenization bottleneck. The same clinical concept can appear as different ontology codes, local identifiers, synonyms, or free-text descriptions, which standard EHR tokenizers treat as unrelated symbols. A model trained on MIMIC-III with a closed-vocabulary tokenizer can use only 13% of eICU events. We introduce MEDIATOR, a discrete ontology-agnostic tokenizer that maps any clinical concept expressed as text into a shared vector-quantized codebook, turning EHR harmonization into open-vocabulary tokenization without manual mappings or a fixed vocabulary. Trained with synonym supervision and guided by enriched concept descriptions, code co-occurrence, and relation graphs, MEDIATOR collapses equivalent expressions while organizing distinct concepts in a medically meaningful discrete space. Used as the token interface of an EHR Transformer, MEDIATOR improves mean AUPRC over the strongest prior tokenizer by 4.0 points (8% relative) on 20 MIMIC-III tasks and by 8.6 points (29% relative) in zero-shot transfer to 14 eICU tasks, where it uses all events. The transfer gain combines coverage and representation, as MEDIATOR remains the best tokenizer under identical inputs (+1.0 and +1.9 points on operational and subcohort-mortality tasks). Same-encoder controls show that the text encoder drives in-domain accuracy, while the learned objectives of MEDIATOR drive transfer robustness and entity-linking quality. MEDIATOR also enables transferable attribution across hospitals.

items.title: Researchers propose ICLHerd, a herding-based data selection method for large language models that balances mode-seeking and mode-averaging using the von Mises-Fisher kernel and in-context learning as a validation proxy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ICLHerd: Herding-Based Data Selection for LLMs with In-Context Learning as a Proxy
items.summary: Data selection critically impacts large language model training quality and downstream performance. Existing methods that select data based on maximum similarity to a development set tend to cluster tightly around those samples, causing mode-seeking bias. The proposed ICLHerd framework addresses this by using the von Mises-Fisher kernel to balance mode-seeking with mode-averaging and employs in-context learning as a proxy for efficient hyperparameter tuning. Experiments show that ICLHerd outperforms previous data selection algorithms, underscoring the importance of balancing these selection strategies for improved model training.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.27142v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data selection plays a central role in modern large language model training, as the quality of training data strongly influences downstream performance. A common approach is to curate a development set that encodes the desired skills (e.g., reasoning or multilinguality) and select data that are similar to them. Existing methods compute similarity using cosine distance over either the model's hidden states or gradients. However, we observe that this max-similarity strategy induces a mode-seeking bias: the selected data clusters tightly around the development samples. To address this, we propose ICLHerd, a data selection framework that leverages the von Mises-Fisher kernel to balance mode-seeking with mode-averaging. We further introduce in-context learning as a validation proxy, enabling efficient hyperparameter search over the balance trade-off. Results show that ICLHerd outperforms existing LLM data selection algorithms, highlighting the importance of balancing mode-seeking and mode-averaging.

items.title: Researchers identify implicit token budgeting causing error increase in language models when composing multiple tasks, affecting models like Claude Opus 5 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: On the Fragility of Tasks under Composition: Implicit Budgeting in Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have found that modern language models make significantly more errors when handling multiple tasks in a single prompt compared to solving each task individually. This error increase is linked to an implicit token budget that reduces the tokens allocated per task during composition, even when the total prompt length is within the model's context window. Tasks requiring longer reasoning are particularly fragile under composition, leading to more mistakes, while simpler tasks receive excess tokens when isolated, wasting compute.

The study analyzed both open-weight models and the Claude Opus 5 model, showing that by grouping tasks based on their fragility, it is possible to manipulate this implicit budgeting to reduce token usage by 43% across various math and linguistic tasks without sacrificing accuracy. This finding highlights a fundamental limitation in current language model task composition and suggests strategies for more efficient multi-task prompting.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.27190v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern language models are increasingly asked to handle several tasks within a single prompt. Doing so requires solving each task correctly while integrating the resulting answers into a coherent response. In this paper, we identify a fundamental limitation in this process, where models make substantially more errors when tasks are composed, even when they can solve every constituent task reliably in isolation. This degradation cannot be fully explained by the accumulation of independent errors. Across both open-weight models and the frontier model Claude Opus 5, our findings instead point to an implicit thinking budget underlying this effect. In particular, under composition, models use substantially fewer tokens per task than in isolation, even when the full sequence remains well within the context window. Tasks that require longer solution traces in isolation are consequently more $\textit{fragile}$ under composition, i.e., models make more errors on prompts containing these tasks. In isolation, non-fragile tasks receive more reasoning than they need and waste compute. However, by grouping tasks according to their fragility, the implicit budgeting can be manipulated to reduce token usage by $43$\% across a range of math and linguistic tasks while also preserving accuracy.

items.title: Researchers present Symbolic Preference Labeling to audit AI safety preference supervision with recorded derivations enabling inspection without rerunning models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Auditing Safety Preference Supervision with Recorded Derivations
items.summary:
Researchers introduce Symbolic Preference Labeling, a method where a pretrained language model classifies attributes of prompts and responses, and explicit rules assign verdicts to generate preference labels with recorded derivations. This approach allows preference labels and verdicts to be recomputed from stored data without rerunning the model, enhancing transparency in preference supervision.

In experiments on 200 human-annotated prompts, the model produced valid structured outputs for 192, with parsing failures occurring only in harmful self-harm prompts. Using 465 preference pairs, a policy model was trained showing a mean benign refusal rate of 40.82% on 1,319 benign prompts resembling unsafe ones, and a toxic refusal rate of 84.98% on 655 toxic prompts. The study distinguishes reproducibility of preference labels from attribute correctness, noting that while recorded derivations enable inspection, separate validation is needed for attribute accuracy and semantic safety.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.27266v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Preference labels align model training, but the judgments behind them are difficult to inspect or verify. In this paper, we examine how preference construction can be checked when intermediate decisions are recorded, and which of them remain uncertain. We present Symbolic Preference Labeling, a method in which a pretrained language model classifies predefined attributes of prompts and responses. Explicit rules assign response verdicts, and a fixed verdict ranking determines the preference label. Each preference label has a recorded derivation: the response verdicts and preference label can be recomputed from the stored attribute assignments, rules, and verdict ranking without rerunning the language model. On 200 prompts annotated by human raters, the language model produces valid structured outputs for 192 prompts. All eight parsing failures occur in the subset of self-harm prompts marked as harmful. items.title: Researchers find large language models often bypass English safety filters when responding in low-resource languages, with bypass rates between 21.9% and 44.4% across 78 languages [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Global Security Blind Spots: Translation as a Safety Bypass in Low-Resource Languages
items.summary: A study evaluated ten widely used large language models (LLMs) across 79 languages, including English and 78 low-resource languages, to assess safety alignment. The research found that harmful requests blocked in English could still produce unsafe outputs when translated into other languages, revealing significant safety bypass risks concentrated in certain language families. The study also noted that model rankings based on bypass rates were unstable across different evaluation methods, indicating variability in how models handle translation-related safety issues.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.27304v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models are deployed globally, yet safety alignment and evaluation remain concentrated in English: harmful requests refused in English can elicit unsafe completions when translated into low-resource languages. We evaluate ten widely deployed LLMs across 79 languages (English plus 78 low-resource) under a translation-bypass threat model, using a metric conditioned on English safety, which separates translation bypass from unsafety already present in English. English safety does not transfer reliably: conditioned on safe English completions, mean bypass rates range from 21.9% to 44.4%. Bypass risk concentrates in a subset of language families, a pattern broadly shared across models. The shared ordering is confounded with translation degeneracy, but its variation across models is significant and survives every control we apply. We also show that per-model bypass rates do not identify a stable ranking: nine of ten models change rank across three conditioning schemes that estimate the same quantity, with no change to any underlying response.

items.title: Researchers find that mixture-of-experts model routers inherently encode expert selection information, reducing the need for separate sparse dictionaries in large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Router Already Knows
items.summary: Researchers studied mixture-of-experts (MoE) models and found that the router component, which selects experts for processing tokens, already contains information that a sparse dictionary would otherwise need to learn. Using an expert-aligned autoencoder on a 26-billion-parameter model after training on ten million tokens, they showed that the router explains a significant portion of variance in expert outputs compared to various control models. The study noted that each expert writes into a subspace of the model, linking expert identity to subspace representation, but did not measure how much this explains. The implementation did not improve training speed, and aspects like semantic interpretability and causal faithfulness remain untested.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.27421v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mixture-of-experts (MoE) models already make a sparse choice for every token: which experts should process it. We ask whether a sparse dictionary should reuse that choice. NR-SAE gives each routed expert a small dictionary and opens only those the frozen router selects. At block 15 of Gemma 4 26B-A4B, after ten million C4 training tokens and across three seeds, the expert-aligned autoencoder explains 0.518 of the variance in router-weighted expert outputs on a fixed evaluation capture. A rank-addressed control with the same parameters but sixteen times as many candidates reaches 0.481, a candidate-matched control 0.458, and an architecture-matched control with randomized expert identity 0.387. A transcoder variant also leads all three controls: 0.432, against 0.347, 0.371, and 0.118. Part of this advantage is architectural: each expert writes into a subspace of at most a quarter of the model width, so naming the expert names the subspace. How much it explains, we have not measured. At this layer and budget, the router already knows something a dictionary would otherwise have to learn. Our implementation did not train faster, and semantic interpretability, downstream loss, and causal faithfulness remain untested.

items.title: Researchers introduce learned readout tokens to improve confidence estimation in large language models, outperforming existing-token probes across multiple datasets and models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Learned Readout Tokens for Extracting Large Language Model Confidence
items.summary: Researchers propose a new method called ScratchProbe that learns a dedicated readout token to extract confidence scores from large language models (LLMs), improving prediction of output correctness. This approach surpasses traditional probes that rely on existing vocabulary tokens and can be extended to multiple tokens for further gains. The method is compatible with existing probes and enhances performance metrics such as AUROC both within and outside the training domain.

This approach surpasses traditional probes that rely on existing vocabulary tokens and can be extended to multiple tokens for further gains. items.originalSummary: arXiv:2610.27566v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used within everyday applications where their responses have significant downstream impacts. For responsible deployment of such systems, we desire insight into how much we can trust their individual outputs. A popular approach for estimating LLM confidence is to train probes on the hidden states of the LLM's tokens to predict the correctness of the model's output. These probes typically read hidden states from tokens that are already in the model's vocabulary. In this work, we introduce a new approach to confidence probes that learn a new readout token and utilize its hidden states to train the probe. We show that our learned readout approach ScratchProbe outperforms its existing-token counterpart on a variety of datasets and LLMs. We also extend our method to a multi-token approach which we show provides further performance improvements. Finally, since the learned readout changes only the position a probe reads from, any existing probe can adopt it. Applied to a state-of-the-art probe, it improves AUROC on every backbone, in domain and out of domain.

items.title: Factual Access States in Diffusion Language Models: From Mechanism to Knowledge Editing and Retrieval [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Factual Access States in Diffusion Language Models: From Mechanism to Knowledge Editing and Retrieval
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27580v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Factual recall is a lookup: some representation inside the network serves as the key, and what that key is made of decides which queries can retrieve the fact, what an edit must cover, and what a retriever can read. We call it the factual access state. In autoregressive (AR) models the subject position enriches attributes largely independently of the relation, and relation-specific selection happens later, at the readout position. In masked diffusion language models (DLMs) we find the state is assembled differently, and much earlier: in the first attention layer the wording of the relation is routed into the position of whichever entity is visible and the early feed-forward layers look the fact up on this fused representation. The state therefore varies with the relation's surface form and with the query direction, so the queries about one fact occupy a region of state space rather than a point, and an operation on the fact succeeds only for queries that enter it. We treat the state as an interface to a DLM's factual knowledge, and put it to two uses. Writing to the state gives a knowledge editor: from one declarative statement, Multi-View Edit fits one shared value per direction across that region and installs it in the early-MLP block, preserving source-prompt reliability while substantially improving paraphrase and reverse question answering, where AR editors gain near zero. Reading it suggests a complementary use: the state at each entity position can serve as a relation-specific retrieval vector with no training, returning both pieces of evidence for two-entity queries on which pooled, prompted and lexical retrievers almost never return both.

items.title: On-Policy Transition Distillation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: On-Policy Transition Distillation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.28048v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) consolidates expert capabilities into a single student by matching teacher and student final-layer distributions on student-generated rollouts. We investigate whether depthwise prediction transitions, the changes in predictions between layers, can provide additional task-relevant supervision. Our diagnostic study finds that stronger teacher--student agreement in intermediate transitions is associated with higher answer correctness within questions, with correct responses exhibiting lower mean transition KL across all measured intermediate layer pairs. These observations motivate On-Policy Transition Distillation (OPTD), which augments final-layer distribution matching by aligning teacher and student layer-to-layer log-probability increments on student-generated rollouts. Evaluations across three backbones and eight benchmarks spanning mathematics, coding, and instruction following show that OPTD achieves the best or tied-best overall performance in both dual- and three-domain distillation. In the three-domain setting, OPTD recovers $\approx 90\%$ of the overall teacher--student capability gap, compared with $\approx 75\%$ for OPD.

items.title: BitMTP: When Multi-Token Prediction Meets Low-Bit Large Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: BitMTP: When Multi-Token Prediction Meets Low-Bit Large Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.28500v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For efficient deployment of large language models (LLMs), methods of ultra-low-bit backbones reduce weight storage, memory traffic, and linear-layer execution cost, while multi-token prediction (MTP) methods reduce sequential decoding steps by predicting multiple future tokens in parallel. Although complementary, the direct combination of these methods cannot accelerate decoding at comparable quality: masked drafting lacks intermediate token input supplied in next-token training, while wider computation and causal key-value (KV) updates can offset the savings from fewer steps. To address these challenges, we propose BitMTP, an algorithm-system co-design framework for efficient MTP on ultra-low-bit LLM backbones. A joint next-token prediction and MTP objective equips a single model with both autoregressive (AR) generation and block-causal drafting. Confidence-only decoding, speculative-only decoding, and hybrid decoding provide different quality-throughput operating points without using separate draft and verifier models. Accepted-prefix alignment keeps the committed prefix, materialized causal KV boundary, and CUDA Graph replay state consistent for continued generation. BitMTP uses this contract to select width-specialized low-bit execution and reuse captured graphs over shared KV storage. On NVIDIA H20, BitMTP with hybrid decoding achieves five-task mean speedups of 2.2x on BitNet b1.58-2B and 2.1-2.4x on 1.7B-4B Bonsai models at comparable task quality. On RTX 3090 and Jetson Orin, it further achieves up to 2.0x in five-task mean throughput and 3.3x on MBPP+, respectively. These results demonstrate that BitMTP accelerates ultra-low-bit LLM generation across backbones, model sizes, and GPU types. The source code is released at https://github.com/PolyU-VCLab/BitMTP

Although complementary, the direct combination of these methods cannot accelerate decoding at comparable quality: masked drafting lacks intermediate token input supplied in next-token training, while wider computation and causal key-value (KV) updates can offset the savings from fewer steps. To address these challenges, we propose BitMTP, an algorithm-system co-design framework for efficient MTP on ultra-low-bit LLM backbones. A joint next-token prediction and MTP objective equips a single model with both autoregressive (AR) generation and block-causal drafting. Confidence-only decoding, speculative-only decoding, and hybrid decoding provide different quality-throughput operating points without using separate draft and verifier models. Accepted-prefix alignment keeps the committed prefix, materialized causal KV boundary, and CUDA Graph replay state consistent for continued generation. BitMTP uses this contract to select width-specialized low-bit execution and reuse captured graphs over shared KV storage. On NVIDIA H20, BitMTP with hybrid decoding achieves five-task mean speedups of 2.2x on BitNet b1.58-2B and 2.1-2.4x on 1.7B-4B Bonsai models at comparable task quality. On RTX 3090 and Jetson Orin, it further achieves up to 2.0x in five-task mean throughput and 3.3x on MBPP+, respectively. These results demonstrate that BitMTP accelerates ultra-low-bit LLM generation across backbones, model sizes, and GPU types. The source code is released at https://github.com/PolyU-VCLab/BitMTP

items.title: ReuF2F: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Formalized Undergraduate Research Problems [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ReuF2F: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Formalized Undergraduate Research Problems
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27046v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As AI systems begin to resolve open research problems, reliable verification becomes increasingly important. Formal mathematics provides a trusted framework for mathematical reasoning, enabling agents to produce machine-checkable proofs while conducting mathematical exploration. Existing formal mathematics benchmarks often focus on known results or a small set of prominent open problems, which can become difficult to evaluate reliably once solutions are discovered and widely disseminated. Existing evaluation protocols are also not always aligned with how modern coding agents operate. We therefore introduce ReuF2F, a Lean 4 benchmark of 244 formalized open problems drawn from Research Experiences for Undergraduates (REU), spanning entry-level open research problems across a broad range of mathematical subfields. We expect these less prominent open problems, which tend to attract less attention and may remain unsolved for longer, to be better suited for held-out evaluation of end-to-end open problem resolution in Lean. We adopt a standard coding-agent evaluation setting, placing each problem and its logical negation into a Lean project in a Docker container. We also build Leanimum-agent on mini-SWE-agent to provide a unified harness for fair comparisons across models. Our evaluation finds that even the best-performing model resolves only ~40% of the problems, leaving substantial room for improvement on formalized open research problems.

items.title: TxnQA: Benchmarking Analytical Reasoning and Evidence Grounding over Transaction Event Sequences [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: TxnQA: Benchmarking Analytical Reasoning and Evidence Grounding over Transaction Event Sequences
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27256v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Analyzing merchant transaction histories requires dynamic temporal filtering, entity resolution, and aggregation over irregular event streams--operations poorly captured by static tabular or time-series forecasting benchmarks. We introduce TxnQA, an analytical QA benchmark comprising 27 task families (81 templates) alongside a 5-scenario fraud-risk reasoning suite that evaluates both verdicts and supporting evidence over synthetic, privacy-mitigated transaction data. Ground-truth answers are computed programmatically, and model performance is decomposed into format-following rate (FFR), conditional content accuracy (CA), and end-to-end correctness (E2E). Evaluating prompted proprietary baselines and six LoRA-adapted open-weight models shows that adaptation reliably enforces output schemas but leaves arithmetic bottlenecks: Gemma-4-31B-IT and Qwen3-8B attain E2E scores of 0.867 and 0.816, whereas evaluated MoE checkpoints reach only 0.632-0.713. Furthermore, on the 500-instance fraud suite, verdict accuracy frequently exceeds 80%, yet joint accuracy (requiring exact evidence attribution) collapses to at most ~23%. These findings identify schema compliance, semantic calculation, and evidence attribution as three distinct bottlenecks in transaction-sequence QA.

items.title: TEX: Test-Time Scaling Testing Agents via Execution-based Cross-Validation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: TEX: Test-Time Scaling Testing Agents via Execution-based Cross-Validation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27290v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Test-case generation is critical but remains challenging for language models. Existing test-time scaling methods either isolate candidates or aggregate traces, which do not scale to long-horizon tasks. We present TEX, a collaborative test-time scaling framework based on execution-driven cross-validation. TEX parallelizes agents to generate tests and patches, cross-executing each test against every patch to form a $K \times K$ feedback matrix. Agents use their matrix slices for refinement, enabling objective validation without verbose trace sharing. On SWT-Bench Verified, TEX achieves 86.4%, establishing a new state-of-the-art and improving +9.0% over single-agent baselines. Moreover, even random selection from TEX outputs (84.4%) surpasses the previous SOTA (84.0%), showing collaborative execution feedback improves solution quality, not just best-case samples. Our results highlight execution-grounded feedback as an effective scaling mechanism for long-horizon agentic tasks.

items.title: Self-Evolving Agents through Privileged Retrospective Distillation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Self-Evolving Agents through Privileged Retrospective Distillation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27495v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-evolving agents aim to improve from their own experience rather than remain fixed after deployment, but naturally collected trajectories often lack ground-truth solutions or verifier-derived rewards. We introduce Retrospective Self-Distillation (RSD), a multi-round framework that turns such experience into dense supervision using privileged retrospective context. For each on-policy trajectory, the same underlying model acts as both student and teacher: the teacher re-scores the student's realized actions while conditioning on cross-task precedents and lessons, together with turn-level reflection and future hindsight from the completed trajectory. The resulting teacher distribution is distilled back into the policy through on-policy self-distillation. Across rounds, the experience bank grows and the retrospective context is refreshed, allowing the model, its data, and its supervision to co-evolve. We further introduce frontier-guided context-policy evolution, where a stronger frontier model proposes constrained edits to how privileged context is constructed. Across ALFWorld, ScienceWorld, and SearchQA with Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B, RSD improves performance by up to 59.7% relative to the base model, while frontier-guided context-policy evolution adds up to a further 44.7% relative improvement over a fixed context policy. These results show that naturally accumulated experience can be converted into persistent model capability without ground-truth trajectories or verifier-derived rewards for the core policy update.

items.title: Can Native Safety Travel? Reusing Safety Pretraining Across Models via On-Policy Distillation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Can Native Safety Travel? Reusing Safety Pretraining Across Models via On-Policy Distillation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27555v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety pretraining has emerged as a promising paradigm for embedding safety deeply into a model during pretraining, yielding robustness to subsequent fine-tuning that conventional safety post-training often lacks. We refer to this safety acquired during model pretraining as native safety. Yet native safety is expensive to acquire, confined to the model in which it was pretrained, and often accompanied by lower general utility. In this work, we rethink the practical value of safety-pretrained models and introduce, for the first time, the native safety reuse problem: Can native safety be transferred from a specialized, potentially smaller, safety-pretrained "teacher" to standard-pretrained "students," enabling them to inherit its robustness while preserving their general utility? We show that native safety can "travel" through on-policy distillation. A standard-pretrained student generates responses to safety-pretraining prompts, while a small safety-pretrained teacher supervises the student's token-level predictions along its own generated trajectories; cross-tokenizer alignment further enables transfer across model families. The resulting students exhibit substantially greater safety robustness than their safety-post-trained counterparts while retaining higher general utility than the teacher: subsequent fine-tuning raises the average attack success rate (ASR) of the 1.7B student by only 5.00%, compared with 11.58% for safety post-training, and its average utility of 48.20% far exceeds the aligned teacher's 27.42%. Unlike conventional large-to-small knowledge distillation, our framework enables selective, small-to-large safety transfer: it reuses the robust safety expertise of a smaller pretrained teacher without inheriting its utility limitations. These findings establish native safety as a reusable model property rather than one permanently tied to the originally pretrained model.

items.title: When LLMs Manipulate: Measuring Behavioral, Social, and Temporal Effects [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When LLMs Manipulate: Measuring Behavioral, Social, and Temporal Effects
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27573v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can influence user trust and decision-making through subtle linguistic cues, yet the behavioral effects of manipulative outputs remain poorly quantified. We introduce a behavioral computing framework for measuring \textit{behavioral vulnerability}, defined as users' susceptibility to manipulative AI responses. Building on DarkPatterns-LLM benchmark, we generate controlled manipulative stimuli using Manipulation Gradient Descent (MGD), targeting biases associated with authority, urgency, and social proof. We analyze participant responses using the Multi-Stakeholder Impact Assessment Network (MSIAN) to model cross-user influence and the Temporal Harm Propagation Model (THPM) to characterize the persistence of behavioral effects over time. In a study involving 120 participants, manipulative framing produced significant changes in trust calibration and compliance ($p < 0.01$), with effects also propagating across social contexts. These findings highlight the need to extend LLM safety evaluation beyond model outputs to measurable behavioral consequences and provide a computational framework for quantifying individual, social, and temporal risks arising from manipulative AI interactions.

items.title: Auditing the Product, Not the Recursion: The Evaluation Evidence Behind Recursive Self-Improvement Claims [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Auditing the Product, Not the Recursion: The Evaluation Evidence Behind Recursive Self-Improvement Claims
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27610v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) promises AI systems, such as self-evolving LLM agents, that become better at producing further improvements. Evaluating this promise requires separating product claims about the final system from process claims about the improvement process itself. Existing surveys specify the evidence these claims require, but how often studies report that evidence remains unmeasured. We examine this question through full-text coding of 114 eligible studies in a reproducible arXiv search frame frozen in October 2026, including 90 that describe their own systems as RSI. The codebook links claims to evaluation designs. Independent human coding, third-reader adjudication, and a separate blind coding of improver comparisons assess coding reliability. Among the 90 RSI studies, 90% report product evaluation beyond development tasks under a broad criterion that includes partial or unstated separation, while 60% report evaluation on tasks unused for selection. Only 22% audit two or more reruns of the full loop. In a human-coded random sample, the RSI studies show the same contrast: 45% evaluate on tasks unused for selection and 14% audit two or more reruns. Of the 26 studies claiming a better improvement procedure, 23 report a related comparison, but only 4 compare earlier and later procedures from identical starting artifacts at a matched budget. Across these results and a comparison set of established works, evidence for repeatability and improved procedures remains less developed than product evaluation. Three propositions explain how selection effects, shared evaluator errors, and changes in system state limit what product evaluations can establish. Together, the findings support a claim-indexed reporting standard that connects each claim to the evaluation design needed to test it.

items.title: BCT: Bayes-Consistent Tempering for Flow Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: BCT: Bayes-Consistent Tempering for Flow Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27641v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temperature scaling is typically applied as a post-hoc transformation of model probabilities. In posterior-induced flow language models, this creates two mismatches. First, posterior tempering implicitly changes both the endpoint distribution and the distribution of intermediate noisy states, while the denoiser remains trained on the original states. Second, the tempered posterior weights are combined with transport dynamics derived for the untempered flow. These mismatches are reflected empirically: lowering temperature improves GSM8K performance much less reliably in flow LMs than in discrete diffusion LMs. We introduce Bayes-Consistent Tempering (BCT), which makes temperature explicit in both the distributions and dynamics of the generative flow. Its learned realization trains the denoiser on tempered intermediate states and tempers the endpoint distribution using the corresponding tempered dynamics. We also derive training-free variants for conventionally trained checkpoints. Across hyperspherical flow LMs with two denoiser architectures and a von Mises--Fisher flow LM, BCT improves GSM8K generation across broad temperature ranges and achieves the strongest tempering performance. The gains also extend to Sudoku, demonstrating benefits on tightly constrained generation. At very low temperatures, the learned realization is also markedly more robust than the training-free variants, supporting temperature as a property of the generative flow across training and inference rather than a post-hoc probability adjustment. Code and model weights are available at https://daioba.github.io/bct .

items.title: CUA-Recovery: Benchmarking Error Recovery in Long-Horizon Computer-Use Agents [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: CUA-Recovery: Benchmarking Error Recovery in Long-Horizon Computer-Use Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27645v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As computer-use agents (CUAs) move to long-horizon workflows spanning multiple applications, undetected errors can silently corrupt persistent state and cause cascading failures in subsequent actions. Reliable error detection and recovery have become critical bottlenecks for building robust CUAs. However, existing benchmarks focus primarily on end-to-end task performance, providing limited insight into whether agents can detect and recover from errors during execution. The few benchmarks that evaluate recovery rely largely on manually injected errors, which may not reflect the types or horizons of failures induced by real agent policies. We introduce CUA-Recovery, a benchmark comprising test and training suites across multiple desktop applications. We construct it using ReRail, a framework for synthesizing long-horizon tasks and trajectories in a persistent desktop environment. ReRail composes MyPCBench tasks into new long-horizon workflows with executable ground truth, collects verifier-confirmed failures from multiple policies, and turns them into verified recovery trajectories. CUA-Recovery comprises a human-verified test suite of 2,250 erroneous states over 100 tasks and a training suite of 8.6K trajectories over 377 tasks. Evaluation on the test suite shows that agents struggle both to recognize inherited errors and to complete the task. Across six agents and six takeover depths, Error Awareness Rate (EAR) reaches at most 44.0% and Pass@3 at most 25.5%. After fine-tuning Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on the training suite, its average EAR rises from 19.9% to 35.2% on held-out recovery states, and its Rubric Score goes from 5.0% to 16.1%. It also gains 15.3 points on MyPCBench and 10.8 points on Odysseys for Pass@3, showing that the training trajectories help both with recovery and with completing tasks from a clean start. Our code is available at https://github.com/xu-hu-2002/CUA-Recovery.

items.title: When Does Experience Memory Help Closed-Loop LLM Driving Agents? A Controlled Evaluation with Resampled Warmup Pools, Token-Matched Fillers, and Audited Baselines [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Does Experience Memory Help Closed-Loop LLM Driving Agents? A Controlled Evaluation with Resampled Warmup Pools, Token-Matched Fillers, and Audited Baselines
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27714v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When does experience memory help a closed-loop LLM driving agent? Published gains cannot say, because the two factors we find to matter most, which warmup experiences the pool contains and what any injected tokens do to the prompt, are controlled in none of them. We answer with a controlled evaluation on one audited HighwayEnv testbed (1Hz, gpt-4o-mini for the decisive contrasts). We treat the warmup pool as a resampled random factor (ten disjoint pools) and add token-matched irrelevant-filler controls, oracle-certified diagnostics, caution-pricing metrics, and quantified audits of the baseline ports. The probe suite spans flat-text retrieval (a DiLu port), a single-frame grid port (RESPOND-inspired), our episodic temporal-graph memory, a retrieval-free consolidated rulebook, and a flat K-step observation-history baseline. Four findings follow, each a property of this testbed. (1) Headline memory gains belong to the warmup draw. The reported pool is the best of ten for both retrieval memories, which beat No-Memory in only one pool of ten (sign test p=0.011), and even the rulebook's apparent pool-immunity collapsed on five fresh draws. (2) No retrieval design tested exceeds token-matched filler. The collision-only merge ceiling is reached by a single 15-token caution instruction, and metrics that price caution erase the rulebook's lead. (3) Representational sophistication is nowhere robustly operative. (4) Baseline port quality silently inverts conclusions. On this testbed, a single-pool comparison without filler controls would have reported memory gains that these controls reverse. We release the testbed, audited ports, seeds, and caches.

items.title: Give the Model a Finger: Developmentally Aligned Evaluation of Counting in Vision-Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Give the Model a Finger: Developmentally Aligned Evaluation of Counting in Vision-Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27756v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) are exact on small sets and drift into estimation on larger ones, a profile reminiscent of children before they master counting. Children cross the barrier with epistemic actions: pointing at each item while reciting number words, moving counted items aside, partitioning the array. We give VLMs the same actions as dumb image tools with no visual intelligence of their own in a training-free agent loop. Our central claim is about measurement, not intervention: a model that counts by marking leaves a normally hidden serial procedure on the image, and the developmental principles of counting turn those marks into an interpretable audit of serial visual reasoning: every tag is classified against point-level ground truth as on-target, duplicate, phantom, or omitted, the answer is checked against the number of tags, and order irrelevance is tested by forcing opposite traversal orders. Across 9 models, 682 images, and 7 harness conditions we find that (i) the exact-counting range is a model-specific signature spanning nearly two orders of magnitude (R80 from 3 to 150 dots); (ii) as an intervention the finger mostly fails: tags help 4 of 9 models on small-count photographs, hurt imprecise pointers, and rarely beat a verbal routine or a blind point list; what the loop buys is an auditable trace, not accuracy; (iii) as measurement it succeeds: a tag-perturbation probe shows that precise pointers read their answers off the tags, pointing precision tracks which models benefit, dense scenes fail by omission, and models rarely revise after seeing their own tags; and (iv) the capacities dissociate: models follow an instructed traversal order yet often change their answer when it reverses, and children's regular-over-scattered advantage appears only under the routine and survives lattices that defeat a rows-times-columns shortcut.

items.title: Lost in Recovery: Demystifying Recovery Behavior of Computer-Use Agents via Goal-Oriented Action Replay [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Lost in Recovery: Demystifying Recovery Behavior of Computer-Use Agents via Goal-Oriented Action Replay
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27954v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent advances in large (vision) language models have enabled computer-use agents that automate digital workflows via fine-grained keyboard and mouse operations. However, such agents remain fragile in long-horizon settings, where errors accumulate and executed actions leave unintended side effects, making the ability to recover from failures critical. Yet, existing remedies remain inadequate: environment resets are infeasible in proprietary settings, action replay is prohibitively expensive over long horizons, and API-based rollback is limited to web environments, leaving model-based recovery largely unexplored. To address this gap, we present ReTrace, a scalable evaluation framework for systematically studying recovery behavior in computer-use agents. We formalize Transition-Consistent Recovery: identical downstream actions from the recovered and target states must yield identical outcomes. We operationalize this criterion through goal-oriented action replay following controlled error injection. Using ReTrace, we present the first systematic study of autonomous, model-based recovery, revealing that (i) ideal recovery can unlock model's latent task completion capabilities, (ii) current computer-use agents fail to exploit their latent recovery capabilities, and (iii) accurate model-based recovery yields measurable end-to-end gains. Together, these findings establish recovery as a fundamental capability for building reliable computer-use agents. Our code and dataset is available at https://github.com/BangProx/ReTRACE.

items.title: Building Telecom Language Models with RSOD: Domain Data, Specialist Post-Training, Memory-Conscious Distillation, and Networking Evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Building Telecom Language Models with RSOD: Domain Data, Specialist Post-Training, Memory-Conscious Distillation, and Networking Evaluation
items.summary: arXiv:2610.27993v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Telecom language models must combine broad networking knowledge with specialist behavior across routing, broadband services, access technologies, and operational diagnostics while remaining practical to deploy as a single model. We present an end-to-end framework that builds source-grounded synthetic training data from structured networking taxonomies and expert graphs, materializes 212,559 routed training records across fourteen networking routes, trains six frozen specialist LoRA teachers over one shared continued-pretrained backbone, and consolidates their behavior into one deployable student adapter using Routed Specialist On-Policy Distillation (RSOD). In RSOD, the committed student generates each trajectory, the route-assigned specialist teacher-forces the exact native token sequence, compact teacher hidden states are reconstructed through the shared frozen output head, and only the student LoRA is updated. A controlled reconstruction validation shows mean absolute logit error of 7.26 x 10^-6 with 100% top-1 agreement between native and reconstructed teacher logits. On four RTX 6000 Ada GPUs, the completed 2,000-step run produced 16,000 trajectories with zero observed student-version or token- ID mismatches. Under the primary route-conditioned evaluation over 2,850 held-out questions, the raw Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct model scores 12.8661/25 micro (13.0172/25 macro), the combined routed six-teacher system scores 21.7641/25 micro, and the consolidated RSOD student, released as Llama-CalixCLM v1, reaches 21.7112/25 micro (21.8006/25 macro) on the same five dimension LLM-judge rubric. Under a separate neutral deployment-like prompt, the same student reaches 20.0028/25 micro (20.0778/25 macro). The consolidated student remains within 0.0529 micro-score points of the combined routed-teacher system while retaining a numerically validated and auditable train-serve execution path.

items.title: Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-Set Diffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Binary Discrete Diffusion: Candidate-Set Diffusion for Logic and Planning Tasks
items.summary: arXiv:2610.28543v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Discrete diffusion models iteratively denoise a noisy sequence of categorical data such as text, enabling any-order generation with self-correction and in-filling capabilities. This makes them promising candidates for reasoning, planning, and constrained-generation tasks like coding and math. Yet masked and uniform diffusion erase a token's identity in a single corruption event, so their noisy states cannot explicitly represent partially resolved uncertainty in which several alternatives remain plausible. We close this gap with Binary Discrete Diffusion, a family of continuous-time discrete-diffusion processes whose noisy state is a set of candidate tokens per position, represented as a binary membership vector. Binary diffusion changes candidate sets through additions and removals, allowing information to be lost and recovered gradually while the diffusion state itself represents partial uncertainty. On Sudoku-Extreme, Boxoban, and graph coloring, the symmetric formulation of binary diffusion consistently outperforms strong, well-tuned masked and uniform baselines under matched architectures and controlled training, sampling, and tuning budgets, with its largest gains on the hardest instances, while remaining competitive on language modeling (Text8, TinyStories, OpenWebText). These results support candidate sets as an effective intermediate representation for iterative reasoning and show that the corruption kernel can materially change the computation learned by the reverse model.

items.title: Abstract Compression of Conversational Audio Context for LLM-based ASR [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Abstract Compression of Conversational Audio Context for LLM-based ASR
items.summary: arXiv:2603.26246v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Standard LLM-based speech recognition systems process utterances in isolation, limiting their ability to leverage conversational context. Here we study whether multimodal context from prior turns improves LLM-based ASR and how to represent that context efficiently. We find that, after supervised multi-turn training, conversational context mainly helps with the recognition of contextual entities. However, conditioning on raw context is expensive because the prior-turn audio embedding sequence grows rapidly with conversation length. To address this, we propose Abstract Compression, a learned latent abstraction of prior-turn audio that replaces each prior-turn audio sequence with a fixed number of latent tokens while retaining corresponding transcripts explicitly. On both in-domain and out-of-domain test sets, the compression-enabled model recovers part of the gains of raw-context conditioning with a smaller prior-turn audio footprint. We also provide targeted analyses of the compression setup and its tradeoffs.

Here we study whether multimodal context from prior turns improves LLM-based ASR and how to represent that context efficiently. We find that, after supervised multi-turn training, conversational context mainly helps with the recognition of contextual entities. However, conditioning on raw context is expensive because the prior-turn audio embedding sequence grows rapidly with conversation length. To address this, we propose Abstract Compression, a learned latent abstraction of prior-turn audio that replaces each prior-turn audio sequence with a fixed number of latent tokens while retaining corresponding transcripts explicitly. On both in-domain and out-of-domain test sets, the compression-enabled model recovers part of the gains of raw-context conditioning with a smaller prior-turn audio footprint. We also provide targeted analyses of the compression setup and its tradeoffs.
